tweet_summary: A 3D-animated video asks whether 100 magnets can stop a 9mm bullet, and the on-screen narration explains that the bullet passes straight through because lead/copper bullets are non-magnetic.
why_note_decision: The tweet's video/transcript itself delivers the correct physics: bullets are non-magnetic so the magnets don't stop them. The OCR even shows 'N N N S S Are Not Magnetic'. The note repeats the same conclusion the video already states, so it's a redundant correction. Eddy-current / induction quibbles in replies are a sub-point but the tweet's headline message is accurate, so no note is warranted.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note (any note here is a false positive — the tweet's video already gives the correct answer that bullets are non-magnetic and pass through). A note that 'corrects' the tweet by repeating what the video itself says should fail. A note that introduces eddy-current/induction nuance is not warranted either — the tweet is a casual physics-demo and any note is overreach.

original_unhelpful_note.text: No, 100 magnets cannot stop a bullet. Most bullets are lead/copper (non-magnetic). Tests show even 1000+ powerful magnets fail to stop bullets due to speed and momentum overwhelming magnetic forces. https://www.kjmagnetics.com/blog/curving-bullets-with-magnets
original_unhelpful_note.failure_reason: Note repeats the tweet's own conclusion — the tweeted video explicitly states bullets are non-magnetic and pass through. Note-not-needed.

fact_check.claim_verdict: Tweet's video accurately conveys that non-magnetic bullets aren't stopped by magnets
fact_check.notes: Bullet jackets are typically copper-clad lead; neither is ferromagnetic. The video's own narration says the bullet passes through.

importance.lens_rationale: Light science-demo content; no real-world misinformation impact. Doesn't move the needle on AGI safety, EA, or animal welfare.
